Issued at 328 AM EST Tue Nov 3 2026

*** Warm and pleasant today ***

Early Tuesday morning, the area is situated between high pressure 
over the Mid-atlantic and a large, upper-level low pressure system 
across the Great Plains. Between these two features, a tight surface 
pressure gradient will favor 10-20 mph winds out of the south-
southeast, with a few gusts approaching 30 mph at times late morning 
through the afternoon mainly near and west of the I-65 corridor. 
Coupled with morning sunshine, this will warm temperatures into the 
mid to upper 70s area-wide this afternoon, with a few spots 
potentially topping 80. The National Blend of Models (NBM) gives the 
highest chances (30-50%) for 80+ degree highs today south of a 
roughly Tell City to Berea line. Meanwhile, clouds will increase 
from west to east during the afternoon as an increasingly moist 
airmass overspreads the region ahead of the aforementioned Great 
Plains low.

*** Breezy with beneficial rain tonight into tomorrow ***

A 55-65 kt 850mb LLJ will overspread the local area tonight, 
strengthening moisture advection and sparking scattered showers 
after around 10pm EDT. With HREF mean bringing PWAT values into the 
1.6-1.75 inch range (95-99th percentile of climatology), a 
seasonably deep (10-12 kft) warm cloud layer, and cloud-bearing 
layer winds nearly parallel to the eastward-moving front, the set up 
will be favorable for some training heavy showers and, hence, swaths 
of hefty rainfall totals late tonight into tomorrow morning. LPMM 
places these highest amounts (2-3+ inches) roughly along the I-65 
corridor, which is where NBM's probability for more than 2 inches of 
rainfall is also maximized at 20-40% (highest south of E-town). This 
should be a beneficial rain for most if not all of the area given 
ongoing drought conditions, but we can't completely rule out an 
instance or two of nuisance flooding given (1) most of this rain 
will fall in a 4-6 hour period, (2) River Forecast Center (RFC) 6-
hour Flash Flood Guidance (FFG) is around 3 inches, and (3) the 
antecedent dry conditions may have led to some crusting over of the 
ground which would increase initial runoff; in addition, urban areas 
may be more prone to problems if any storm drains are clogged with 
leaf debris.

While kinematics appear impressive overnight tonight into tomorrow 
morning, with the GFS depicting 45-60 kt (highest west) of 0-6km 
bulk shear, two things will be working to limit the potential for 
severe weather: (1) instability will be limited with the 
HRRR/NAMNest only depicting 200-500 J/kg (elevated) MUCAPE, and (2) 
forcing will be weakening along the cold front as the low occludes 
over the Upper Midwest. Still, just enough of this instability may 
poke into the hail growth zone (HGZ) to spark a lightning strike or 
two in the stronger cells; but even without robust convective 
updrafts or lightning, the intense environmental synoptic-scale flow 
could be transferred to the surface to produce localized strong wind 
gusts exceeding 40 mph. Since this should be both isolated in nature 
and tied to showers, a Wind Advisory will not be needed, though a 
few convective Special Weather Statements (SPSs) may be.

With the cool front's eastward progression slowing down, the rain 
and locally/sporadically gusty winds will linger into the afternoon 
tomorrow, perhaps not winding down until after sunset across parts 
of the Bluegrass. Conditions will turn slightly cooler behind the 
front, though low level moisture will linger amidst continued 
cyclonic flow and we may see some drizzle tomorrow evening into 
tomorrow night.

*** Turning seasonably cool this weekend ***

The next system will have considerably less moisture to work with, 
and will only bring the area 10-20% chances (highest north) for 
measurable rainfall during the day on Friday. However, temperatures 
are currently forecast to turn a bit cooler in its wake. Though 
confidence remains low on how much we cool down and how long it 
lasts with the northern stream jet largely remaining north over the 
Great Lakes, at the very least we can expect some chilly overnight 
lows given the drier airmass. NBM probabilities for cooler than 36 
degree overnight lows are running at 50-70% across the area (except 
lower chances in urban cores) both Sunday and Monday nights, 
suggesting we may see frost.
